messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Nguyen is a 28-year-old Vietnamese American tax consultant who presented for psychological assessment approximately seven months after an experience of captivity that left her PCL-5 score at 74, placing her firmly in the severe range of post-traumatic stress. She is single, lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment, and described herself, before the trauma, as someone who prided herself on competence and self-sufficiency.

The incident occurred when Linh was returning to her car in a parking structure after working late at her firm. Two men forced her into a vehicle at gunpoint, and she was held for nearly eighteen hours in a residential basement before being released. During that time she was physically restrained, moved between rooms without warning, and subjected to repeated unpredictable intrusions — men entering the space at irregular intervals, sometimes silently, sometimes loudly. She was released without explanation and without any of the men ever facing legal consequences, a fact the police confirmed to her weeks later when the investigation stalled.

Since her release, Linh has developed a vigilance that organises her entire day. At her office, where she sits in an open-plan workspace, she has quietly maneuvered her desk chair so that her back is always against a partition wall and she can see the full length of the floor. Colleagues have noticed but said nothing. When a coworker rounds a corner quickly or a door swings open unexpectedly, her body responds before her mind can intervene — a sharp flinch, a surge of adrenaline, her hands going still over the keyboard. At home, her evenings are spent in a particular corner of her couch, her back to the wall, listening for sounds at the front door — a creak, a footfall on the landing, anything that might mean someone is entering. She has begun sleeping with a chair wedged under her door handle.

What the heightened threat monitoring does, in ways Linh finds harder to articulate but no less real, is feed a corrosive internal narrative about herself. Each time she flinches at a sudden movement in the office, she reads her own reaction as evidence — proof that she is broken, that something essential in her has been permanently altered. She had come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that the captivity had happened because of the way she had acted: that she had been too trusting walking to her car alone, too slow to react, too compliant once restrained. In her mind, her body's ongoing failure to feel safe confirmed this logic — if she had been stronger, smarter, more capable, none of it would have happened, and she would not now be sitting at a desk flinching at shadows. The shame she carries about what was done to her body during those eighteen hours sits alongside this self-blame without displacing it; they occupy the same interior space, reinforcing each other in silence. And the knowledge that the men responsible face no consequences — that they are, as far as she knows, entirely free — makes the self-blame worse, because if no external accounting exists, then the only explanation that remains is her own culpability.

The vigilance and the self-reproach have together narrowed her world considerably. She has declined two client dinners, avoided the parking structure her firm uses, and stopped answering her door without first checking the peephole twice. A friendship with a colleague has cooled because Linh cancelled plans repeatedly without explanation, and she has noticed her supervisor commenting on errors in her work — errors she attributes to the hours she spends listening, scanning, bracing.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a moment at the office three weeks ago when a fire drill sent the building into sudden noise and movement and she found herself pressed against the wall in the stairwell, unable to move, certain something terrible was happening. A colleague stayed with her until she could breathe again. She said, quietly, that she was most afraid the clinician would confirm what she already suspected — that this was her fault, and that she would feel this way forever.
